newsitem.title: GERMANY: East Germany cannot compete if wages rise - Rexrodt.
newsitem.headline: East Germany cannot compete if wages rise - Rexrodt.

text.p: Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt warned on Thursday that raising wages in Germany's former Communist east in line with their western equivalents could hurt the east's competitive position.
But the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said the government had failed to keep its promise to help east Germany catch up quickly with the more affluent west.

In an address marking six years since German unification, Rexrodt told parliament unit wage costs in east Germany were too high compared to those in the west. Eastern workers had to focus on raising productivity, he said.

"There is no way round the economic principle: you can only pay wages in proportion to output. If you ignore this, you endanger competition and corporate health," said Rexrodt, a week after Germany celebrated Unity Day on October 3.
"There is no room for undifferentiated wage increases and rapidly bringing wages to the same level," he said.
But SPD deputy Anke Fuchs told the lower house Bonn had failed to address many problems in the east which were getting worse.

"A spontaneous economic upturn in east Germany is farther away than ever. The vast structural and unemployment problems are not decreasing," she said. "The promised rapid convergence of living standards in east and west remains far from sight."
Fuchs said the consequences were more bankruptcies, alarmingly high unemployment, ineffective training schemes and rising crime and social despair.
Rexrodt, however, argued progress had been made despite this year's economic slowdown there.

He said average wages had crept up to some 80 percent of those in the west, workers' output had more than doubled since 1991, and 500,000 small to medium-sized firms in east Germany now employed some 3.4 million people.

Last month, Rexrodt said Bonn would continue to pump a high level of state aid into east Germany after a government report showed that the region had still to overcome the legacy of 40 years of central planning.
The report said east Germany was still beset by high unemployment, unit labour costs over 30 percent higher than in the west and a weak industrial base and infrastructure.

New funds for the former Communist east would be transferred once existing subsidy plans wind up over the next two years. German net transfers to the east will total a massive 144 billion marks ($95.54 billion) this year and 138 billion marks in 1997.
